ops.new_text: # A decoder branch for the cardiac component of lung EIT: a preregistered, parameter-matched evaluation across measurement-noise levels

**Abstract** — In lung electrical impedance tomography (EIT) the cardiac component is small and lung-dominated; the semi-Siamese U-Net added a decoder branch for it. We asked whether that branch alone, at matched parameter count and supervision with fixed 1:1 loss weights, improves cardiac separation and how that depends on measurement noise. Two preregistered studies used EIDORS simulations reconstructed with the Graz consensus algorithm (GREIT). The second registered heart-channel Dice as primary endpoint, five arms of 58 seeds, a primary signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 40 dB and an evaluation-only sweep, 60 to 20 dB. At 40 dB the registered rules returned no benefit: the early-branch arm led its capacity-matched control by 0.223 Dice points (95% CI 0.020 to 0.441), below the registered floor of 0.670 (p = 0.098). The registered noise hypothesis was confirmed: for 40 dB-trained networks the advantage grew by 1.937 points from 60 to 20 dB (CI 1.400 to 2.465), with onset between 35 and 30 dB and the lung channel flat. A registered addendum retrained both arms at 20 dB: with training matched to evaluation the advantage fell 9.2-fold, to 0.229 points (CI 0.081 to 0.373), below its floor of 0.384, because retraining alone recovered most of it. The branch therefore pays off for a network trained at 40 dB and evaluated under heavier noise, not when training matches evaluation: most of that benefit is mismatch tolerance. Trained at its operating level, the network gains 0.22 to 0.23 points at both levels and clears the registered floor at neither.

Chest EIT reconstructs conductivity change over the thorax from boundary voltages, and its clinical use, from regional ventilation monitoring to titration of ventilator settings, rests on the ventilation signal (Frerichs et al., 2017) <!--ref:Frerichs2017TREND--><!--anchor:none:-->. The cardiac-related signal in the same frames carries information of its own. Regional perfusion measured by EIT, and in particular its mismatch with ventilation, was an independent predictor of mortality in a prospective cohort of patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome (Spinelli et al., 2021) <!--ref:Spinelli2021CritCare--><!--anchor:none:-->, and perfusion EIT has been reviewed as a route to detecting pulmonary embolism (Nguyen et al., 2012) <!--ref:Nguyen2012PhysiolMeas--><!--anchor:none:-->. That signal is small. In normal human lungs tidal breathing changed resistivity by about 9%, while the change over the cardiac cycle was between 0.9% and 2.6% and varied by region (Leathard et al., 1994) <!--ref:Leathard1994PhysiolMeas--><!--anchor:none:-->, and its amplitude depends strongly on position in the thorax (Graf and Riedel, 2017) <!--ref:Graf2017PLOSONE--><!--anchor:quote:highly%20position%20dependent-->. It is also not perfusion itself: in a piglet model, regional perfusion estimated from the first pass of a hypertonic bolus agreed with single-photon emission tomography and was superior to the estimate from impedance pulsatility (Borges et al., 2012) <!--ref:Borges2012JAP--><!--anchor:none:-->, so what any frame-wise method recovers is the cardiac-related component of the image, not a measurement of regional blood flow. On the simulated phantom used throughout this paper, the point about size can be made with one measurement rather than an assertion. Applying the quarter-amplitude threshold that clinical region-of-interest methods use (Pulletz et al., 2006) <!--ref:Pulletz2006ROI--><!--anchor:none:--> to the mixed lung-plus-heart reconstruction recovers the lung at a mean Dice coefficient of 0.951 against its own reconstruction over 3,600 frames. The same threshold recovers the heart at a mean of 0.099 and a median of 0.000 (Fig. 2 shows the frame at that median). The cardiac component is not merely faint in these images. On more than half of the frames, the standard threshold finds nothing at all. Throughout, we use *segmentation* for the task of producing a mask and scoring it with Dice, and *separation*, *weak component* and *dominant component* for the mechanism of extracting the cardiac signal from the mixture.

In current practice the cardiac-related signal is separated from the ventilation signal in time, not in a single frame. The impedance changes synchronous with the heart rate are of very small amplitude (Frerichs et al., 2009) <!--ref:Frerichs2009--><!--anchor:quote:impedance%20changes%20synchronous%20with%20the%20heart%20rate%20are%20of%20very%20small%20amplitude-->, and the methods used to recover them all work on the pixel time series. Electrocardiogram-gated averaging over cardiac cycles came first, with applied potential tomography, where the low signal-to-noise ratio of the cardiac signal already required acquisition synchronised to the heart and averaging in time (Eyuboglu and Brown, 1988) <!--ref:Eyuboglu1988CPPM--><!--anchor:none:-->. Frequency-domain filtering followed, on the observation that the ventilation and perfusion components occupy separable bands, so that about fifteen seconds of data could replace the hundred or more cardiac cycles that gated averaging needed (Zadehkoochak et al., 1992) <!--ref:Zadehkoochak1992CPPM--><!--anchor:none:-->. Together with breath holding and principal-component methods these are the standard routes (Nguyen et al., 2012) <!--ref:Nguyen2012PhysiolMeas--><!--anchor:none:-->, listed as breath holding, electrocardiogram-gated averaging and frequency filtering (Grant et al., 2011) <!--ref:Grant2011--><!--anchor:quote:breath%20holding%2C%20electrocardiograph%20(ECG)%20gating%20and%20frequency%20filtering-->, or template fitting that combines principal component analysis with frequency filtering to give a beat-by-beat cardiac signal after a short set-up period (Deibele et al., 2008) <!--ref:Deibele2008--><!--anchor:quote:electrocardiogram-gated%20averaging%2C%20frequency%20domain%20filtering%20or%20holding%20the%20breath-->. Compared on the same animal data against a contrast bolus as reference, frequency filtering outperformed ensemble averaging, and both performed similarly during ventilation and during apnoea (Stowe et al., 2019) <!--ref:Stowe2019PhysiolMeas--><!--anchor:none:-->. The current model-based line is adaptive harmonic estimation, whose authors name spectral and spatial overlap between the cardiac and respiratory components as a limitation of the existing methods (Silva et al., 2025) <!--ref:Silva2025TBME--><!--anchor:none:-->. A learning-based temporal method also exists: a Siamese network trained on breath-hold image series supplied a feature-matching constraint for unsupervised separation of the cardiac-related component from a chest EIT image series, with separated images qualitatively consistent with nuclear perfusion scans in three patients (K. Zhang et al., 2022) <!--ref:Zhang2022PhysiolMeas--><!--anchor:none:-->. Each of these methods needs a time series long enough to resolve the two rates, and the Siamese method separates a series, not a frame. The frame-wise approach studied here is not proposed as a replacement for them and is not compared with them. It answers a narrower question inside the frame-wise approach: whether one architectural element of it, the dedicated decoder branch, does the work attributed to it.

Those three studies sit inside a wider EIT deep-learning literature. Deep learning entered EIT first at the reconstruction step. Learned reconstruction from voltages has been reviewed under three headings, a single network, a network combined with a conventional algorithm, and hybrids of several networks (T. Zhang et al., 2022) <!--ref:Zhang2022FBB--><!--anchor:none:-->, and for the thorax a supervised descent method compared its accuracy and noise resistance against Gauss–Newton inversion on synthetic data and gave results broadly consistent with CT on measured chest data (K. Zhang et al., 2021) <!--ref:Zhang2021TBME--><!--anchor:none:-->. A second line keeps a conventional reconstructor and places the network after it. Deep D-bar post-processed D-bar reconstructions with a convolutional network trained on simulation and applied it to experimental data without transfer training (Hamilton and Hauptmann, 2018) <!--ref:Hamilton2018TMI--><!--anchor:none:-->. A graph U-Net trained on simple two-dimensional simulations post-processed reconstructions from devices of different geometry and instrumentation, including three-dimensional measurements (Herzberg et al., 2023) <!--ref:Herzberg2023PhysiolMeas--><!--anchor:none:-->. A network trained on pairs of scattering transforms and organ boundaries recovered the boundaries of heart and lungs together within the D-bar framework (Capps and Mueller, 2021) <!--ref:Capps2021TBME--><!--anchor:none:-->. The present paper belongs to this second line. Every input is a GREIT reconstruction, and the network's task is separation after reconstruction. Multi-branch networks have also appeared in EIT reconstruction, where a segmentation branch and a reconstruction branch were fused to recover conductivity on lung-shaped data, with tolerance of measurement noise and modelling error as a stated aim (Yu et al., 2024) <!--ref:Yu2024CMPB--><!--anchor:none:-->.

What none of the three prior studies did is isolate that branch. A second decoder adds parameters, and a second supervised target is a well-known regulariser in its own right (Caruana, 1997) <!--ref:Caruana1997MTL--><!--anchor:none:-->. The original comparison bundled both with the weighted loss. In the multi-task learning literature the arrangement used here, one shared encoder feeding task-specific decoders, is the standard encoder-focused design for dense prediction, and its known failure mode is task interference, in which the gradients of one task degrade the shared features that another task needs (Vandenhende et al., 2022) <!--ref:Vandenhende2021--><!--anchor:none:-->. Where the branches should separate has no general answer, which was the starting point of cross-stitch networks (Misra et al., 2016) <!--ref:Misra2016CrossStitch--><!--anchor:none:-->, and the one study we found that compares branching structures under a fixed budget of learnable parameters built its branches from task affinity, sharing the shallow layers and separating the deeper ones (Vandenhende et al., 2020) <!--ref:Vandenhende2020Branched--><!--anchor:none:-->. It is the nearest methodological precedent for the parameter-matched contrast used here. The usual remedy for interference is to weight the task losses, by hand, by a learned per-task uncertainty (Kendall et al., 2018) <!--ref:Kendall2018--><!--anchor:none:-->, or by a dynamic average that follows each task's rate of loss change (Liu et al., 2019) <!--ref:Liu2019MTAN--><!--anchor:none:-->. Weighting and branching are therefore two answers to one problem, and the original semi-Siamese study used both at once. This study fixes the weights at 1:1 and varies only the branch. Equal fixed weights are not a naive default: two independent studies reported at the same conference found that minimising the plain sum of the task losses, with the regularisation used in single-task training, matches or beats specialised multi-task optimisers (Kurin et al., 2022) <!--ref:Kurin2022Unitary--><!--anchor:none:-->, and that current multi-task optimisation methods did not outperform a tuned weighted average across language and vision tasks (Xin et al., 2022) <!--ref:Xin2022MTOHelp--><!--anchor:none:-->. Whether weighting can substitute for branching is the subject of a companion study and is not tested here. Any uncontrolled comparison between a branched and an unbranched network mixes capacity and supervision into the branch itself. The point is not specific to EIT: a re-examination of three-dimensional medical image segmentation found that claims of new architectures outperforming a U-Net often rested on inadequate baselines and did not survive rigorous validation (Isensee et al., 2024) <!--ref:Isensee2024nnUNetRevisited--><!--anchor:none:-->. Comparisons of multi-decoder architectures are also commonly made at a single noise condition, which leaves open whether the result would survive a different one. Benchmarks of segmentation networks under systematic corruptions found that tolerance of corruptions differs between architectures and depends strongly on the corruption type (Kamann and Rother, 2021) <!--ref:Kamann2021IJCV--><!--anchor:none:-->, and that current networks for MRI segmentation are highly sensitive to simulated distribution shifts, including changes of signal-to-noise ratio (Boone et al., 2023) <!--ref:Boone2023NeuroImage--><!--anchor:none:-->. The term *dual-branch* also carries a different meaning in the EIT reconstruction literature. In the dual-branch U-Net of Wang et al. (2024) <!--ref:Wang2024TIM--><!--anchor:quote:the%20encoder%20involves%20two%20branches%20for%20shape%20modeling-->, the two branches sit on the encoder side and feed one fusion decoder that reconstructs conductivity from voltages, and the multi-branch network of Yu et al. (2024) <!--ref:Yu2024CMPB--><!--anchor:none:--> likewise fuses a segmentation branch with a reconstruction branch to recover conductivity, whereas the branch examined here sits on the decoder side and serves one output each. Within the scope of our search, which covered the three prior studies, Crossref title queries of 2026-09-23, and title-and-abstract queries in OpenAlex, Crossref, PubMed and Semantic Scholar on 2026-10-06 for EIT deep learning, cardiac-component separation, multi-task decoders and noise tolerance under distribution shift (search strings in the project repository), we are not aware of a comparison in which the decoder branch is evaluated at matched parameter count and matched supervision across several measurement-noise levels, nor of a study that takes the multi-decoder versus single-decoder contrast at matched capacity as its subject. The nearest adjacent work in EIT is the original semi-Siamese study itself, and the nearest in multi-task learning is the fixed-budget branching study above.

Training settings were fixed before registration and not tuned per arm: Adam at 1 × 10⁻³ with cosine decay to 1 × 10⁻⁵, batch size 16, at most 200 epochs with early stopping on validation loss (patience 20, best weights restored), L1 loss on the float target with no output activation, loss weights 1.0/1.0, no augmentation, and one dataset-wide normalisation affine estimated from the training split (full settings and software environment in Supplementary S7). No noise augmentation was used: every training frame carried the registered 40 dB level, so that the evaluation-only sweep measures the response to levels the network had not seen. Drawing measurement degradation at random during training is the other established choice in EIT, used with simulated measurement noise and model error for shape reconstruction (Ren et al., 2020) <!--ref:Ren2020TIM--><!--anchor:none:-->, with unspecified poor electrode contact for cardiac-output estimation (Murphy et al., 2019) <!--ref:Murphy2019PhysiolMeas--><!--anchor:none:-->, and with electrode displacement for wearable thoracic EIT (Jeschke et al., 2025) <!--ref:Jeschke2025Sensors--><!--anchor:none:-->. Section 2.7 describes the one condition in which the training level was changed. The backbone is a U-Net (Ronneberger et al., 2015) <!--ref:Ronneberger2015UNet--><!--anchor:none:-->. All 290 runs (five arms by 58 seeds) executed on one machine (Mac mini M4), because splitting across machines would place hardware differences inside the paired contrasts.

Within those limits the evaluation-only shape is still informative about the measurement chain. The obvious alternative, that the flat top is the Dice ceiling compressing a real but small effect, does not hold: with each seed's gain expressed as a fraction of the control arm's own remaining error, the high-SNR intervals contain zero and the intervals from 35 dB down exclude it. The seed-level structure points the same way, since the seeds that benefit most at 40 dB are not those that benefit most at 20 dB (ρ = −0.10). The registered primary level therefore lies above the onset on this phantom, and "under threat" can be given an operational reading from the same numbers: at 40 dB the control arm still recovers the cardiac component at a Dice of 0.966, and at 20 dB it has lost 8.8 points on that component and 2.0 on the lung. What the addendum adds is that the threat, so defined, is largely a threat to a network that has not seen the noise before. Trained on it, the control arm recovers 8.0 of the 8.8 points on its own, and the branch is left with the same 0.2 points it was worth at 40 dB. The counter-argument raised in the pre-submission review, that distribution shift and weak-component threat make the same prediction in an evaluation-only sweep, was correct, and the experiment registered to separate them has answered it: the larger part of the evaluation-only advantage is distribution-shift tolerance. In the vocabulary of Castro et al. (2020) <!--ref:Castro2020NatCommun--><!--anchor:none:-->, the evaluation-only sweep is an acquisition shift between the data the network was developed on and the condition it was tested in. That the training noise sets the tolerance of such a shift is known elsewhere: discriminative image denoisers were typically trained for one noise level each and lacked flexibility across levels, the limitation that FFDNet removed by taking a noise-level map as an input (K. Zhang et al., 2018) <!--ref:Zhang2018FFDNet--><!--anchor:none:-->, and appropriately tuned Gaussian noise during training improved generalisation to unseen corruptions in image classification (Rusak et al., 2020) <!--ref:Rusak2020ECCV--><!--anchor:none:-->. We regard this as the most useful result in the paper, because it is the one that a study without the addendum would have reported the other way round.

That sentence is about this measurement chain, not about the branch. The reconstructor decides how much measurement noise reaches the image, and that dependence has been a figure of merit of EIT reconstruction since the regularised linearised inverse of Adler and Guardo (1996) <!--ref:Adler1996TMI--><!--anchor:none:-->, which defined noise amplification and derived the probability of detecting a contrast as a function of measurement noise and reconstruction algorithm. GREIT let a tenfold change in noise amplitude move the reconstructed input by a median 8.5% of peak, and that 8.5% cost the control arm 8.8 heart-Dice points when the network had not been trained on it. A different reconstructor, a thoracic rather than cylindrical geometry, real electrode contact, or a different noise spectrum would each change where a given instrument SNR lands relative to the onset, and this study measured none of them. Whether a real measurement chain sits above or below the onset is therefore not determined here. The 40 dB primary level was registered as a conservative operating point by the laboratory's convention and does not correspond to a particular instrument. If a real instrument delivers a higher SNR to the reconstructor, the negative result at the operating level becomes stronger, not weaker, because the network sits further above the onset. A practitioner who wants to place a chain on this curve has a recipe in the numbers above: measure the image-domain perturbation that the reconstructor passes at the operating SNR, compare it with the 8.5% median peak fraction reported here, and ask whether the deployed network was trained at that level. If it was, this study gives no reason to expect the branch to add more than a fraction of a Dice point. The post-reconstruction line this network belongs to has reported generalisation across instruments when the network is trained on simulation (Hamilton and Hauptmann, 2018 <!--ref:Hamilton2018TMI--><!--anchor:none:-->; Herzberg et al., 2023 <!--ref:Herzberg2023PhysiolMeas--><!--anchor:none:-->). The present result does not bear on that cross-instrument generalisation. It concerns a change of noise level within one instrument model and one reconstructor, and it shows that at that change the training level, not the architecture, decided most of what happened.

The practical lesson is for anyone comparing architectures rather than for anyone treating patients. For a network trained at 40 dB, the branch is worth 2.1 Dice points on the cardiac channel at 20 dB, with dz above one, and 0.2 points at 40 dB, where it fails a preregistered rule. For a network trained at 20 dB it is worth 0.2 points at 20 dB and fails the same rule. A study that ran only one of those conditions would have reported its number as the answer, and an uncontrolled comparison, in which capacity and supervision travel with the branch, would have had no way to tell which side of the onset it was on. The condition dependence is the finding, and it is visible only because the arms were matched, the sweep was registered, and the retrained contrast was registered before it was run. The same logic runs in the other direction. A study that matched the arms and registered its rule but sampled only the registered primary level would have concluded, correctly by its own rule, that the branch does nothing, and would have missed the regime in which it does. And a study that ran the sweep without the retrained contrast, as this one did before its addendum, would have attributed to the branch what belongs mostly to the training condition. The lesson has precedents on both sides of the measurement chain. On the instrument side, measurements on a resistive mesh phantom found that the SNR of an EIT system depends on frame rate, operating frequency, injected current and measurement strategy, and the authors concluded that performance figures should always be reported together with those parameters (Gagnon et al., 2010) <!--ref:Gagnon2010TBME--><!--anchor:none:-->. On the network side, benchmarks of segmentation models under controlled corruptions found that tolerance of corruptions differs between architectures and depends strongly on the corruption type (Kamann and Rother, 2021) <!--ref:Kamann2021IJCV--><!--anchor:none:-->, and that networks for MRI segmentation are highly sensitive to simulated distribution shifts, among them changes of SNR (Boone et al., 2023) <!--ref:Boone2023NeuroImage--><!--anchor:none:-->. An architectural comparison reported at one noise level and one training condition is, by those results and by this one, a comparison at one point of a surface.

The original semi-Siamese study attributed its gain to the interaction between the branch and the multi-task weighting and did not separate them. It also did not match capacity or vary noise, and its conclusions list the separation effect under different reconstruction algorithms as future work (Ko and Cheng, 2021b) <!--ref:Ko2021PLOSONE--><!--anchor:quote:the%20separation%20effect%20of%20the%20EIT%20image%20obtained%20by%20the%20different%20reconstruction%20algorithms%20will%20be%20investigated-->. Taking the branch on its own, this study finds no effect at 40 dB and a large one at 20 dB. That does not contradict the original. It isolates one of the two components the original proposed together, under conditions the original did not test, and it leaves the weighting, and the interaction the original described, untested here. The design itself belongs to a family that is common in medical image analysis, one shared encoder feeding task-specific up-sampling branches, of which the nuclear segmentation and classification network HoVer-Net is a widely used member (Graham et al., 2019) <!--ref:Graham2019HoVerNet--><!--anchor:none:-->. What this study adds to that family is not a new member but a controlled measurement of what one member's branch is worth, and under which conditions.

Three of the fifty-three references are to our own group. That ratio is structural rather than elective. The architecture under test is our own, and the study exists to evaluate it under controls its original description did not include.

Seven limitations bound the claims. First, one reconstructor and one noise model: every input was produced by GREIT, whose regularisation removed most of the measurement noise before image space, and reconstructors with different regularisation would present the network with a different perturbation at the same nominal SNR. The noise was additive and Gaussian on the voltage frame, whereas electrode-area and contact-impedance errors produce ringing, field-wide artefacts and structural distortion rather than noise of that kind (Boyle and Adler, 2011) <!--ref:Boyle2011PhysiolMeas--><!--anchor:none:-->, so the sweep says nothing about those error sources. Second, fixed loss weights: the original architecture and the 2025 study used weighted losses, and this study did not compare the branch against weighting or test whether one can substitute for the other. Third, one phantom and no measured data. The study is simulation-only by design, because the registered rules need a ground-truth cardiac image for every frame and a noise level that can be set exactly and re-set across a sweep, and a measured recording provides neither. The cost is that the position of any real measurement chain relative to the onset is unmeasured, and a single cylinder with simply parameterised organs is not a thorax. Fourth, one modality, and one target: what the branch separates is the cardiac-related component of the image, which is not a measurement of perfusion (Borges et al., 2012) <!--ref:Borges2012JAP--><!--anchor:none:-->. Fifth, the addendum retrained only the two primary arms and only at 20 dB, so the matched-training result is known at two levels, 40 and 20 dB, and the shape of the advantage under matched training between them is not measured. Sixth, the onset shape and the channel specificity were not registered tests, and reproducing either as a finding requires a pre-specified decision rule. Seventh, a second decoder may act as a regulariser of the shared encoder rather than as a specialist for its target, the role an added reconstruction branch played in a brain-tumour segmentation network trained on limited data (Myronenko, 2019) <!--ref:Myronenko2019AEReg--><!--anchor:none:-->. The present design cannot separate the two readings, and shows only that, whichever it is, the effect is small when training matches evaluation. The statement under test is a conditional. Each of its conditions is separately falsifiable, and this study tested one cell of that grid. The companion conditions remain to be tested.

The corresponding author is the original author of the semi-Siamese U-Net evaluated in this study. Three of the fifty-three cited works are from the authors' group. The ratio follows from the study's purpose, which is to evaluate the authors' own architecture under controls its original description did not include. The authors declare no other competing interests.
